newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu returns to his frightened capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu returns to his frightened capital.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, returned on Thursday to his frightened capital where residents braced for what many believe is an inevitable battle for the city.

State television showed Mobutu, who is fighting cancer and a seven-month-old civil war, descending the steps of his plane on the arm of his wife Bobi Ladawa one day after efforts to stage peace talks on a South African ship in Congo collapsed.
"Bloodbath" was a word on many lips in Kinshasa, the final target of Laurent Kabila's rebels, as the teeming city of five million people prepared for the worst.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath. It's a question of balance of forces. Kabila knows he has the upper hand," said Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna.
"Confrontation is inevitable. We will have two or three bad days from now on," Mobutu opponent Mukendi wa Mulumba said.
Shops were shuttered and businesses closed early. The normally bustling streets emptied ominously well before sundown and a third night of military curfew.
Mobutu's flight may prove the last into the city. An airline office in a downtown hotel said that the airport, which is 25 km (16 miles) from the centre of the city, was effectively closed.

Witnesses said the road to the airport was eery and largely deserted, apart from increasingly jittery and aggressive members of security forces. The last commercial flight, South African Airways, left on Wednesday.
An unconfirmed report, in a city where rumours circulated wildly, said the airport had been fired on.
Officals in Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo, said ferry services across the river from Kinshasa had halted. One official said Zairean customs officers had shut their offices.
South Africa's Nelson Mandela, who has been trying to avert a battle for Kinshasa, cancelled Wednesday's planned shipboard summit after Kabila, citing security concerns, failed to show.
But despite the misgivings in Kinshasa, where residents fear a rampage by Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined army as much as anything else, mediation efforts continued.
Kabila, whose forces control three-quarters of Africa's third largest nation but who said he would only meet Mobutu at sea, held talks with Mandela in Cape Town.
Mobutu has dominated what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries since seizing power in 1965, reputedly ammassing a huge fortune on the way.

He agreed at peace talks on May 4 to hand power to an elected president. Kabila, then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Rebel justice "commissioner-general" Mwenze Kongolo, quoted by Portugal's Lusa news agency on Thursday, said Mobutu ran the risk of capture if he remained in power until Saturday.
The government maintains that rebel forces are being held up by the army some 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa. The rebels say they are much closer to the city.
The opposition newspaper La Reference Plus feared the worst. "Big dictators only negotiate their departure on the basis of a bloodbath," it said in an editorial.
Across the river in Brazzaville, U.S., British, French, Belgian and Portuguese troops waited to pluck foreign nationals to safety should the battle for Kinshasa begin.
